Fragmenta in epistulam ad Philippenses (in catenis)
Phil: Prolog
̓Εν ταύτῃ τῇ ἐπιστολῇ κληρικοῖς γράφει οὐ λαϊκοῖς· δι' οπερ οὐδὲ πλειόνων ἐδεήθη
ἠδικῶν, σπουδὴ δὲ αὐτῷ διὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς τὸ τῆς ταπεινοφροσύνης κατορθωθῆναι
ἐν αὐτοῖς. δι' αὐτῆς δὲ τῆς παραινέσεως δείκνυσιν αὐτῶν τὸ ἀκριβὲς τοῦ αλλου βίου.
σπανίως γάρ τις καὶ ἁμαρτάνει καὶ φυσιοῦται· τὸ γὰρ τῆς φυσιώσεως απτεται τῶν
κάλλιστα βιούντων καὶ ὑπ' αὐτοῦ τούτου ὡς τὰ πολλὰ ἐπαιρομένων. Phil 1,7
Πανταχοῦ καὶ διὰ πάντων δείκνυται οὐκ ἀνόνητά μου τὰ παθήματα οὐδὲ αἱ
ἀπολογίαι. ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας πίστεως ἀπόδειξιν ποιοῦμαι τὴν ὑμετέραν ενστασιν.
thought_title: Paul writes to clergy to cultivate humility
orientation: Oecumenius opens his commentary by explaining the audience and purpose of Paul's letter to the Philippians.
pass_a_gloss: In this letter he writes to clergy, not to laity; for which reason he did not need more of wrongs, but his effort through the letter was that the thing of humility be set right among them. And through the exhortation itself he shows the exactness of their other life. For rarely does someone both sin and be proud; for the thing of pride touches those who live most nobly and who for the most part are lifted up by this very thing. Everywhere and through all things my sufferings and my defenses are shown not to be without profit. From your faith I make a proof, your steadfastness.

choices.why: Glossary term; the main virtue Paul seeks to cultivate in the Philippian clergy.
Glossary term; the vice that especially attacks those who live well.
Glossary term; the Philippians' firm stand in faith used as proof of Paul's fruitful suffering.
Keeps the negation and the sense of fruitlessness; matches the argument that Paul's sufferings are shown to be fruitful.
Literal rendering of the middle/passive participle; preserves the image of self-exaltation tied to pride.

bible_refs.note: Paul's sufferings and defenses shown not to be without profit, and the Philippians' faith and steadfastness as proof.

pass_b_english: In this letter Paul writes to clergy, not to laity. For this reason he did not need many moral corrections. His concern through the letter is that humility be set right among them. By the very advice he gives, he shows how exact their conduct is in every other respect. For it is rare for someone both to sin and to be proud. Pride takes hold of those who live the best lives and who, for that very reason, are usually lifted up by it.
Everywhere and through everything Paul shows that his sufferings and his defenses are not without profit. From your faith, he says, I draw proof of your steadfastness (Philippians 1:7).

last_rejected.why: Glossary requires 'pride' for φυσίωσις/related forms. 'to be proud' uses 'proud' not 'pride'; the glossary bans 'self-importance' but 'proud' is not the fixed term.
last_rejected.ruling: φυσιοῦται means 'to be proud/inflated'; 'to be proud' is within normal range. No evidence glossary fixes this verb form to noun 'pride'.

problems.quote: From your faith, he says, I make your steadfastness my proof
problems.why: Faith and steadfastness swapped as source/proof across sections; reader loses track of Paul's logic.
problems.fix: Clarify which is means and which is evidence.

variants.text: From your faith, he says, I make your steadfastness my proof
I do it from your steadfastness
I do it from your faith

edits.old: From your faith, he says, I make your steadfastness my proof
edits.new: From your faith, he says, I draw proof of your steadfastness

fixed: The English already says the same thing as the source: faith is the basis from which Paul draws proof, and steadfastness is what is proven. The wording 'I make your steadfastness my proof' could be misread as making steadfastness the evidence, so I clarified it to 'I draw proof of your steadfastness' to keep the logic clear.
